clue.text: Rheingold mostly replaced by new Wagner opera

indicators.note: most of a word is all of it bar the last letter, so the final one never arrives
to be re-placed is to be put somewhere else, and letters put somewhere else spell something else

parts.note: the title of the first opera in Wagner's Ring cycle, handing over all but its last letter
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.walkthrough: Both titles are Wagner's, so the italicised one reads as a fact to recognise rather than raw material — and it is a letter short of what is needed, which is where 'new' comes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Wagner opera -> LOHENGRIN: definition by example — Wagner wrote thirteen operas, and this is the 1850 one about the knight who arrives in a swan-drawn boat.

clue.text: Theatrical event: Material Girl's introduction made it wild

indicators.note: what runs wild is under nobody's control, and letters out of control will not stay in the order printed

parts.note: eight letters thrown into the mix

indicators.note: an introduction comes at the very front, so only the opening letter of the name beside it is taken

parts.note: the letter the name starts with
six more letters, from the two small words that follow

explanation.walkthrough: The italics make Material Girl a Madonna single, so it looks like a reference to be known; the possessive is the giveaway, since it is the Girl's opening letter that joins in.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatrical event -> LEGITIMATE DRAMA: the trade's name for straight spoken plays staged live, as against musicals, variety or film.

clue.text: Describing classic story in full? Not quite

parts.note: to be in is to be at home

indicators.note: not quite the whole word, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: rich can mean full, as of a rich (full-bodied) flavour

explanation.surface: A question about whether a classic tale has been told completely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in full' looks like a single phrase about telling a story completely, but 'in' and 'full' each give their own piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Homeric is the adjective for the epic poems attributed to Homer, the Iliad and the Odyssey.

clue.text: Symbolic writing in religious texts held by country

indicators.note: what is held by something sits in its grip, so these letters go inside the other piece

parts.note: a nation is a country, the people and the state together
OT is the Old Testament, the older half of the Bible

explanation.walkthrough: OT for the Old Testament is a convention worth owning: a setter can call it scripture, books of the law or religious texts and mean those two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Symbolic writing -> NOTATION: the system of signs music, chess and maths are written in, where each mark stands for a thing rather than a sound.

clue.text: Early travel writing? Free to engage in surreal tripping

indicators.note: one word engaging in another sits inside it
tripping suggests a hallucinatory trip, so the letters of surreal are scrambled

parts.note: to rid is to free

explanation.surface: A wry suggestion that early travel writers were free to describe hallucinogenic journeys.
explanation.walkthrough: Rural Rides is William Cobbett's 1820s account of riding through the English countryside, which is why the definition calls it early travel writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Cobbett's book is a classic piece of nineteenth-century travel journalism, early by the standards of the genre.

clue.text: Tuck into this lunch, finally, after noon

indicators.note: what comes finally comes at the end, so each word hands over the letter it closes on
coming after something means being written behind it, which settles where this piece lands

parts.note: N is the short form for noon, as on a timetable
the letter each of those three words finishes on, in the order they stand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tuck into this lunch' reads as one invitation to eat, and only its first word is the definition; the rest of the phrase is there to be dismantled.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuck -> NOSH: British slang for food — a school tuck shop sells it — and both words mean grub rather than the act of eating it.

clue.text: Aim of mountaineering clubs attracting member …

indicators.note: whatever attracts a thing draws it up against itself, so the two pieces finish side by side

parts.note: C is the card table's letter for clubs
a limb is a member of the body, the older sense of the word

explanation.walkthrough: The dots at the end run the sentence into the next clue and carry no letters with them. A card suit and a leg are the two senses hiding in ordinary words.
explanation.definitionFit: Aim of mountaineering -> CLIMB: what a mountaineer sets out to make is an ascent, and the noun names both the act of going up and the route taken.

clue.text: Relative, American, coming into money

indicators.note: whatever comes into a place is inside it once it arrives, so this piece sits in the middle of the other

parts.note: a coin is money you can hold in your hand
US is the standard short form for the United States

explanation.walkthrough: The commas make 'Relative, American' one description of a person, so the definition looks longer than it is: the first word alone is doing that job.
explanation.definitionFit: Relative -> COUSIN: your aunt's or uncle's child is one particular degree of kin, so the definition names the class the answer belongs to.

clue.text: Very hot area — I never will import non-flowering plant

parts.note: the pronoun read as the single letter it is written with

indicators.note: to import goods is to bring them in across your borders, so this piece is carried inside the other

parts.note: 'Never!' and 'No!' are the same flat refusal, so one stands in for the other
ferns spread by spores and never flower, which is why they answer that description

explanation.walkthrough: The dash sets up a sentence somebody is speaking, and the refusal in the middle of it is really two letters that open up to take a plant inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Very hot area -> INFERNO: Dante's name for hell, used since of any raging blaze, so the phrase describes the place entirely by the heat in it.

clue.text: Strikes table end, getting drunk? It's just a bit of fun

indicators.note: a drinker on the way home cannot hold a straight line, and neither can these letters hold their order

parts.note: fifteen letters from the three words, exactly the length the grid wants

explanation.walkthrough: Skittles is the pub game of bowling at wooden pins, so the drinking and the table belong to the picture; every letter comes from the first three words.
explanation.definitionFit: just a bit of fun -> BEER AND SKITTLES: the idiom for easy pleasure, nearly always heard in the negative — life is not all beer and skittles.

clue.text: … draw recalled around morning range

indicators.note: to recall a thing is to call it back, and letters called back come the other way
a piece set around another wraps outside it, leaving a gap in the middle to fill

parts.note: to draw a rope is to tug it, and that word is set down the other way about
AM marks the hours before noon on a clock

explanation.walkthrough: The dots carry the sentence on from the clue before and bring no letters with them. 'Draw' is a tug of war here, not a picture, which is the pivot of the whole clue.
explanation.definitionFit: range -> GAMUT: the whole sweep from one end of a scale to the other, originally the complete musical scale, now any full span of possibilities.

clue.text: Change of membership upset Liberal in new arrangement, mostly

indicators.note: the plainest container word there is: what is 'in' something has the other letters standing on either side of it

parts.note: to arrange things anew is to reset them, and the last letter is left off

indicators.note: most of a word is all of it bar the final letter, which is left behind

parts.note: somebody in a huff is upset and sulking about it
L is the party's letter on a ballot paper

explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' sits right beside a political party and looks like an instruction to jumble it. It is a word to translate instead, and the party gives up a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Change of membership -> RESHUFFLE: a prime minister who reshuffles the cabinet refills the same posts with different people, which changes who belongs to it.

clue.text: Suppress outrageous Latin penned by trio, cutting end

indicators.note: a pen is what livestock are shut into, so whatever is penned finishes up enclosed

parts.note: a trio is three, with the last letter of the number cut off

indicators.note: the end of a word is the letter it finishes on, and cutting takes that letter away

parts.note: over the top, OTT for short, is what outrageous behaviour gets called
L is the dictionary's tag for a Latin word

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is three people writing something outrageous in Latin. 'Penned' is the farmyard sense, and 'trio' is a number waiting to be spelled out.
explanation.definitionFit: Suppress -> THROTTLE: to throttle is to choke off a flow — a voice, fuel to an engine — so both words mean holding something down until it stops.

clue.text: America is backtracking about mistake in Hispanic mountains

indicators.note: to backtrack is to retrace your steps, so these letters are read the way they came
a piece set about another goes round it, with the second one nested inside

parts.note: A is the short form for America, with the two letters of the word beside it
to err is to make a mistake

explanation.walkthrough: 'America is backtracking' reads as a headline about a retreat, and that is exactly what the letters do. 'Hispanic' is pointing at a Spanish word rather than a place.
explanation.definitionFit: Hispanic mountains -> SIERRA: the Spanish word for a saw-toothed mountain range, at home in Spain and Latin America — Sierra Nevada, Sierra Madre.

clue.text: One with a headache: curious uprising keeping Nigeria unsettled

indicators.note: an uprising goes up, and in a down clue up means reading the letters from the bottom

parts.note: a rum business is a curious one in British usage, and the word is read up the grid

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold on to it, so this piece closes round whatever it holds
what is unsettled will not stay where it was put, and these letters leave the order given

parts.note: the seven letters of the country, put in a different order

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a news bulletin about political unrest, which keeps you looking for a country rather than for letters. 'Rum' for curious is a standing crossword sense.
explanation.definitionFit: One with a headache -> MIGRAINEUR: the clinical term for a person subject to migraines, built from the condition plus the French ending for one who does something.

clue.text: Revealing garments? I'm turning crimson, randomly clutching one

indicators.note: turning into something else means changing form, and here it is the letters that change theirs
at random means with no order at all, so no letter keeps the place the clue gave it
to clutch a thing is to grab it and hold it close, so it ends up gripped in the middle

parts.note: the two letters of the contraction, as printed
seven more letters, the colour of a blush
one is the Roman numeral I, a single stroke

explanation.walkthrough: Turning crimson is blushing on the surface, and the clue means it literally of the letters. The number in the last word is the piece they close around.
explanation.definitionFit: Revealing garments -> MICRO-MINIS: skirts cut even shorter than a miniskirt, so brief that the name doubles up on how little cloth is involved.

clue.text: Fish biting line in Arctic

indicators.note: a fish that bites closes its mouth round what it takes, so this letter finishes up inside

parts.note: a cod is the fish on the fishmonger's slab
L is the abbreviation for line, as in a page reference

explanation.walkthrough: A fish taking the line is a whole fishing picture, and 'biting' belongs to it twice over — it is also what the answer does to your face.
explanation.definitionFit: Arctic -> COLD: weather called arctic is bitter enough to recall the polar region, so a proper noun does duty as a plain adjective.

clue.text: Co-ordinate basic manoeuvres before fool shows up

indicators.note: the first piece comes before the second in the answer
manoeuvres here means moves around, so the letters of basic are rearranged
in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top, i.e. backwards

parts.note: an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: Simple manoeuvres being carried out ahead of a fool turning up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Co-ordinate' reads like a verb about organising the manoeuvres, but it is a noun from graph geometry.
explanation.definitionFit: The abscissa is the x-value of a point on a graph, one of its two coordinates.

clue.text: It's a big book in my opinion

parts.note: 'in my opinion' and 'to my mind' say the same thing, so this little word turns into that one
the one whose opinion it is, shrunk to the speaker alone

explanation.walkthrough: 'In my opinion' looks like the setter hedging about how big the book is. It is not a comment on the definition at all — it is the whole of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: a big book -> TOME: a tome is a weighty volume, the word you reach for when a book is thick enough to prop a door open.

clue.text: Spooner's plan for water incursion: protective item on vehicle

indicators.note: Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the first sounds of the two words are exchanged

parts.note: a flood is an incursion of water
a map is a plan

explanation.surface: Reads like a flood-risk planning document that oddly ends up as a car accessory.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words are FLOOD MAP; swapping their opening sounds FL and M gives MUD FLAP.
explanation.definitionFit: A mud flap hangs behind a wheel to stop spray and stones being thrown up from the road.

clue.text: Distress? Try a holiday after resort's closure

indicators.note: one thing after another is written behind it, which is how these two pieces line up

parts.note: a court that tries a case hears it, so the two verbs meet in the courtroom

indicators.note: the closure of a word is where it shuts, so the letter wanted is its last

parts.note: the letter that word shuts with
a break is a holiday, a week away from work

explanation.walkthrough: 'Try a holiday' reads as advice from a kind friend, and every word of it is wordplay: the definition is the single word at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Distress -> HEARTBREAK: grief at its sharpest, the distress of a love or a hope that has gone, so the two nouns match in kind and in weight.

clue.text: Ecstasy, as it happens, will keep our group undefinable

parts.note: E is the tabloid letter for the drug ecstasy

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold on to it, so this piece closes round what comes next

parts.note: a broadcast as it happens is live
the group that takes in the speaker is us

explanation.walkthrough: The comma makes 'as it happens' sound like the setter's aside when it is a broadcaster's term, and the drug at the front is standard crossword shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: undefinable -> ELUSIVE: what is elusive slips away whenever you reach for it, so a quality nobody can pin down in words is exactly that.

clue.text: Europium and vanadium in mineral? A lot of work here

indicators.note: the small word doing container duty: what is 'in' a thing has the rest of it standing either side

parts.note: ore is the rock a metal is mined out of
Eu is europium's symbol in the periodic table
V is vanadium's symbol in the same table

explanation.walkthrough: Two elements out of the periodic table hide behind a sentence about mining, and the question mark admits that one rock is standing in for the class.
explanation.definitionFit: A lot of work -> OEUVRE: an artist's oeuvre is the entire body of what they made, the French for work taken into English art criticism.

clue.text: Medic protecting society members, heading off trickster

indicators.note: to protect somebody is to stand round them, so this pair shelters the letters between them
a word's heading is the letter at its front, and heading off is that letter leaving

parts.note: Dr is the title a medic answers to
a lodge is a branch of a society such as the freemasons, and the word covers its members too; the front letter goes

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a doctor keeping a club's names quiet. A lodge is a local branch of a society and also the people in it, which is what makes 'society members' fair.
explanation.definitionFit: trickster -> DODGER: one who dodges gets out of duties and trouble by cunning — Dickens's Artful Dodger is the type of the word.

clue.text: Reduced price: initial 99% reduction for this nobleman

indicators.note: the initial letter, D, is the Roman numeral 500; cutting it by 99% leaves 5, the Roman numeral V

parts.note: a discount is a reduced price

explanation.surface: Like a sale sign promising enormous price cuts on a title.
explanation.walkthrough: In Roman numerals D is 500 and V is 5, so a 99% reduction of the initial D turns it into V.
explanation.definitionFit: A viscount is a peer ranking above a baron and below an earl.

clue.text: Stone containing aluminium compound

indicators.note: a container holds its contents within its walls, so these letters sit between the outer pair

parts.note: st is the abbreviation for the stone, the British fourteen-pound weight
Al is aluminium's symbol in the periodic table

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a geologist's rock with metal in it. Both pieces are abbreviations instead, one off a set of scales and one off the periodic table.
explanation.definitionFit: compound -> SALT: in chemistry a salt is what an acid and a base make between them, so the general word covers it by class.

clue.text: Cushion a large rise, ignoring first time

indicators.note: to ignore something is to pass over it, and 'first' says which of the two matching letters is passed over

parts.note: the article taken as the single letter it is written with
L is the size on a clothing label
to levitate is to rise off the ground, and one of its two Ts is dropped
t is the scientist's symbol for time, and it is the letter taken out

explanation.walkthrough: 'A large rise' sounds like a pay claim and 'ignoring first time' like a lenient magistrate. Both are instructions about letters, and neither is about money or mercy.
explanation.definitionFit: Cushion -> ALLEVIATE: to cushion a blow is to soften it, and to alleviate is to make a pain or a burden easier to bear.

clue.text: Eddy, man embracing wife and student

indicators.note: to embrace somebody is to put your arms right round them, so this letter finishes up inside

parts.note: sir is how you address a man you do not know
W is the family tree's abbreviation for wife
L is the plate a learner driver carries

explanation.walkthrough: Eddy opens the clue with a capital letter, so he reads as the man in the sentence; the definition is that first word and the family scene is decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: Eddy -> SWIRL: an eddy is water turning in a circle, and a swirl is that same curling movement, so the two nouns name one thing.

clue.text: Sufficient number in survey? Not initially

indicators.note: the initial is the letter at the head of the word, and 'not' strikes that one out

parts.note: the number a survey questions is its sample

explanation.walkthrough: 'Number in survey' looks like an instruction to put something inside, and the 'in' is only part of the phrase for what a pollster questions.
explanation.definitionFit: Sufficient -> AMPLE: ample is as much as is needed and a little over, so it covers the same ground with room to spare.

clue.text: Promises danger to thirty, wanting one Earl replaced by Australian

indicators.note: a thing wanting is a thing missing, so the letter named next is the one no longer there
a replacement takes over the seat the old one had, so the length is untouched — a swap, not an extra

parts.note: thirty counted out as three lots of ten, written in words rather than figures
Earl is E among the peerage abbreviations, and this is the letter that leaves
A is the standard short form for Australian, as on a cricket scorecard

explanation.walkthrough: 'Thirty' is not a number to turn into Roman letters here but a sum to write out in words, and the peer is there to supply a letter for eviction.
explanation.definitionFit: Promises danger -> THREATENS: a sky that threatens rain promises trouble rather than a gift, so 'promises' is taken in its ominous sense.
